origin_region: Shan State · Namhsan and the Palaung hills (also Pindaya, Ywangan and Kalaw)
cultivar: Assamica-type tea bushes and trees of the Shan hills, seed-grown, many of them old
processing: Young leaves are steamed briefly, packed tightly into bamboo tubes, jars or lined pits, weighted and left to ferment without air for several months; the pickled leaves are then washed, sometimes kneaded with oil and salt, and sold wet, to be eaten as a salad or with condiments.
harvest_season: Spring leaf (April to May, after the first rains) makes the best laphet; the pickling takes months, so the new season's product reaches the market in summer and is sold through the year.
appearance_dry: Not dried: a dark olive-green, glossy, moist mass of soft whole leaves, usually sold in vacuum packs or by weight from a tub, with a sour, grassy, pickled smell.
appearance_liquor: Not brewed; the dressing in the salad is oil, lime and garlic rather than an infusion.
appearance_wet: Soft, dark green, slightly slimy pickled leaves, whole or coarsely chopped.
taste_profile: Sour, grassy and bitter with a deep lactic tang and a lingering tea astringency; mixed with sesame oil, fried garlic, crunchy beans, peanuts, tomato and lime in laphet thoke it becomes savoury, bright and addictive.

brewing.notes: Laphet is eaten, not brewed. For a salad, mix a spoonful of the pickled leaf with sesame oil, fried garlic, crispy beans, peanuts, sesame, tomato, chilli and lime. Steeping a few rinsed leaves gives a sour, thin infusion of curiosity value only.

vintage_note: Sold fresh as a pickled food, not by vintage: by grade (tender spring leaf for eating plain, coarser leaf for salads), by region (Namhsan is the famous name) and by brand, in vacuum packs and ready-mixed salad kits with the condiments in separate sachets. Keeps for months refrigerated once opened; there is no ageing culture.
description:
Myanmar is the one country where tea is a food as much as a drink. Laphet is pickled tea leaf, eaten with the fingers as a snack, offered to guests on a lacquer tray, served at the end of a meal, and mixed into laphet thoke, the tea leaf salad that is the country's best-known dish. Most of it comes from the Palaung hills of northern Shan State, around Namhsan, where the tea gardens are old and the hills steep.

The leaf is picked young, steamed just enough to soften it, then packed tightly into bamboo tubes, jars or lined pits and weighted down, so that it sours for months in the absence of air; the best spring laphet is sometimes left longer. It comes out dark green, glossy and tangy, and is then washed, sometimes kneaded with a little oil and salt, and sold wet. It is a post-fermented tea in the technical sense, a cousin of Thai miang and Japanese goishi-cha, but it has never been a drink.

On its own it tastes sour, green and bitter with a lactic depth and the unmistakable grip of tea. The classic way to eat it is with a tray of condiments: fried garlic, crunchy fried beans and peas, peanuts, toasted sesame, dried shrimp, a little chilli. In laphet thoke the leaf is tossed with those plus shredded cabbage, tomato and lime, and the sour-bitter-savoury combination is as moreish as it sounds. It is mildly stimulating, which is part of its hospitality logic: tea is what you give a guest to keep the conversation going.

It is sold in vacuum packs by region and brand, plain or ready-mixed as salad kits, in Burmese groceries and increasingly abroad. Tender spring leaf for eating plain costs more than the coarser salad grade. The same hills also make dry tea for drinking, laphet chauk, which Burmese teashops pour free as 'plain tea' alongside the sweet milk tea.

If you have only had the salad in a restaurant, try the plain pickled leaf with fried garlic and sesame and nothing else; that is how the tea itself tastes.
sources_note: Category 'heicha' chosen because laphet is a microbially post-fermented tea leaf product; 'other' would be the alternative. Fermentation times are the commonly stated range (months); some producers use shorter or longer pickling.
